planting.note: Set container-grown plants out in spring once frost danger has passed, into humus-rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in a shaded or part-shaded site.

directions: This South American understory vine from the temperate rainforests of Chile and Argentina climbs by twining stems lined with small, glossy, trifoliate leaves. Boquila has drawn horticultural and scientific attention for its unusual leaf mimicry, altering leaf size, shape, color, and venation to resemble the foliage of whatever host shrub or tree it is climbing on. Small inconspicuous cream flowers appear in leaf axils but rarely set fruit outside its native range. Grow in constant shade with evenly moist, humus-rich soil and shelter from drying wind and hard frost; where winters are too cold for outdoor culture it performs well as a container or conservatory vine trained on a moss pole or small trellis.

planting.note: Plant in spring in fertile, well-drained soil against a wall, fence, or tree trunk in partial shade; provide support as tendrils have only weak adhesive pads compared to Boston ivy.

directions: Native to woodland margins across the Himalayan region from Afghanistan to western China, this relative of Boston ivy climbs by tendrils and is prized for new growth that emerges in coppery bronze-purple tones before maturing to green, then turning rich red and purple in autumn. Small greenish flowers in summer are followed by inedible blue-black berries on female plants. It tolerates part shade better than full sun, where strong light can scorch the colored young foliage, and is well suited to a woodland-edge wall, pergola, or old tree trunk where its understated seasonal color display can be appreciated at close range. Established plants need little care beyond occasional pruning to control spread.

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring against masonry, a sturdy fence, or large trellis in well-drained soil; self-clinging adhesive pads need no tying once established.

directions: 'Robusta' is a long-grown, extra-vigorous selection of Boston ivy noted for larger, thicker-textured three-lobed leaves and faster wall coverage than the common species form. Like the species it clings tightly to brick, stone, and masonry via adhesive-tipped tendrils, needing no support once anchored, and produces inconspicuous summer flowers followed by small blue-black berries that attract birds in fall. Foliage turns a strong orange-to-scarlet in autumn before dropping to reveal the bare, woody framework beneath. Because of its exceptional vigor it is best reserved for large walls, parking structures, or sound masonry that can carry its weight, and growth should be kept clear of windows, gutters, and roof shingles.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs
North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Not recommended for planting; included here for identification and removal reference only.

directions: Oriental bittersweet is a vigorous, dioecious, woody twining vine native to East Asia that was widely planted in North America for its showy autumn display of yellow capsules splitting open to reveal orange-red arils, before its invasive behavior became apparent. It tolerates woodland-edge partial shade as a seedling and juvenile vine, then climbs into full sun in tree canopies where its girdling stems can kill mature trees and its abundant bird-dispersed seed allows it to overrun native forest understory, displacing the similar-looking native American bittersweet (Celastrus scandens). It is classified as a noxious or invasive plant and banned from sale or planting in numerous US states. This entry is included for identification purposes so it can be distinguished from the native species and targeted for removal, not as a planting recommendation.
sources: USDA Forest Service Weed of the Week
Invasive Plant Atlas of the United States
